newsitem.title: INDIA: INTERVIEW - Revival steps planned for India shipping.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Revival steps planned for India shipping.

text.p: India plans to boost its shipping industry's uneven performance with a multi-pronged strategy involving financial incentives and maritime training programmes, director general of shipping Michael Pinto said.
A report on a major new shipping policy, covering import and financing regulations for the purchase of new ships, was being finalised, he told Reuters in an interview.
"I hope to have a report out very soon," Pinto said. "We hope it will come out within a month."
"We're trying to cover all the issues. We want to make sure that no issue, however slight, is not covered," he added.
Pinto said the Indian shipping industry's performance had been uneven for a very long time.
India's shipping tonnage has been stagnant at around 7.0 million grt (gross registered tonnage) for the last 10 years. At the end of April 1997, it stood at 6.88 million grt.
Officials of the Indian National Shipowners' Association (INSA) say the shipping industry scrapped more tonnage than it had added over the years.
"Partly the reason is because this is a cyclical industry, it's an industry in which perhaps adequate incentives have not been given, and we need to see separately what needs to be done," Pinto said.

Indian shipowners say financial burdens imposed by taxes and high interest rates have handicapped them while freer rivals steamed into Indian ports hungry for a share of the growth in cargo that followed reforms, begun in 1991.
INSA has pleaded for tax and duty reliefs and an annual allocation of $300 million for commercial borrowings for shipping. But it is still awaiting a response from the finance ministry.
"There is a mismatch between the length of maturity required by the Indian government and the length of maturity that is available to the shipping industry," Pinto said.
Unless this problem was resolved soon, he said, it would be difficult for Indian shipowners to raise funds abroad.
"The whole idea of external commercial borrowing is going to be a non-starter unless we can address this question," Pinto said.

Indian shipowners can raise foreign currency loans through financial institutions like the Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India. But they are still at a disadvantage compared with foreign competitors for whom the cost of funds works out cheaper.
Indian shipowners also say they are under pressure from foreign lines that lure seafarers with far higher salaries than they can afford to pay.
Pinto said this would continue to be a perennial problem.
"They pay more wages, and this is something we will always have to live with," he said.
India plans to combine its four different maritime training institutes under the single umbrella of a maritime university, Pinto said.
"Our intention is that these four should come together under one umbrella and get the status of a deemed university, and we are working on the question of bringing them together," he added.
